d.g: Full of zeal; ardent, fervent; exhibiting enthusiasm or strong passion, particularly in matters of religion.

zealous.e: From Middle English zelose, from Latin zēlōsus, from zēlus + -ōsus, from Ancient Greek ζῆλος (zêlos, “zeal, jealousy”), from ζηλόω (zēlóō, “to emulate, to be jealous”). By surface analysis, zeal + -ous. Doublet of jealous.

d.g: Of or pertaining to a zenith.
Azimuthal.

zenithal.e: English zenith Proto-Indo-European *h₂el-der.? Proto-Italic *-ālis Latin -ālisbor. Old French -albor. ▲ Latin -ālis Old French -elbor. ▲ Latin -ālisbor. Middle English -al English -al English zenithal From zenith + -al.

d.g: The cardinal number occurring before one and that denotes no quantity or amount at all, represented in Arabic numerals as 0.
d.x: The conductor waited until the passenger count was zero.

d.g: The numeric symbol that represents the cardinal number zero.
d.x: In unary and k-adic notation in general, zero is the empty string.

d.g: The digit 0 in the decimal, binary, and all other base numbering systems.
d.x: One million has six zeroes.

d.g: Nothing, or none.

zero.e: Collectively borrowed from Early Modern Spanish zero, Middle French zero, and (their etymon) Old Italian zero, from Medieval Latin zēphirum, from Arabic صِفْر (ṣifr, “nothing; cipher”), itself calqued from Sanskrit शून्य (śūnyá, “void; nothingness”). Doublet of cipher and chiffre. …

d.g: In the initial position in a sequence whose elements are numbered starting at zero; the ordinal number corresponding to zero.
d.x: The zeroth order polynomial approximation is constant.

d.g: Corresponding to a position preceding the first.
d.x: A and C are in equilibrium following the Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics.

zeroth.e: English zero English -th English zeroth From zero + -th (ordinal suffix).

d.g: Of food, or an aroma or flavour: pleasantly piquant, pungent, or spicy; zesty.

d.g: Having a spirited love of life; ebullient, zesty.

zestful.e: From zest + -ful (suffix forming adjectives from nouns, with the sense of being full of, tending to, or thoroughly possessing the quality expressed by the noun).

d.g: Having a piquant or pungent taste; spicy.
Zestful.
(of a man) Flamboyantly or effeminately gay.
Gay.

zesty.e: English zest Proto-Indo-European *-kos Proto-Germanic *-gaz Proto-West Germanic *-g Old English -iġ Middle English -y English -y English zesty From zest + -y.

zealously.e: English zealous Middle English -ly English -ly English zealously From zealous + -ly.

zestily.e: English zesty Middle English -ly English -ly English zestily From zesty + -ly.

zeal.e: From Middle English zele, from Old French zel, from Late Latin zēlus, from Ancient Greek ζῆλος (zêlos, “zeal, jealousy”), from Proto-Indo-European *yeh₂- (“to search”). Related to jealous.

a native or inhabitant of Zealand
One who is zealous, one who is full of zeal for their own specific beliefs or objectives, usually in the negative sense of being too passionate; a fanatic.
d.x: For Modes of Faith let graceleſs zealots fight; / His can't be wrong whoſe life is in the right:

d.g: A member of a radical, warlike, ardently patriotic group of Jews in Judea, particularly prominent in the first century, who advocated the violent overthrow of Roman rule and vigorously resisted the efforts of the Romans and their supporters to convert the Jews.
A member of an anti-aristocratic political group in Thessalonica from 1342 until 1350.

zealot.e: Initially only found as Middle English zelote, an epithet of Simon the Zealot, acquiring its current senses in the 16th and 17th centuries. …

d.g: Something characteristic of a zealot; excessive zeal; fanaticism.

zealotry.e: English zealot English -ry English zealotry From zealot + -ry.

zeaxanthin.e: From New Latin Zea (genus name of Indian corn) + xanthin.

zebra.e: First attested in 1600. Borrowed from Italian zebra, from Portuguese zebra, zebro (“zebra”), from Old Galician-Portuguese enzebro, ezebra, azebra (“wild ass”), from earlier cebrario (882), ezebrario (897), from Vulgar Latin *eciferus, from Latin equiferus (“wild horse”) (Pliny), from equus (“horse”) + ferus (“wild”). …

d.g: Any wood with a figure (grain pattern) like the striping of a zebra, most often wood of the genus Microberlinia.
A domesticated ox native to Asia and Africa, having a large fleshy hump on its back and a dewlap (Bos taurus indicus).

Fell out of usage in England by the 17th century, and made standard in the U.S. in American Dictionary of English Language by Noah Webster in 1828, though usage varied for decades afterwards.

zeitgeist.e: Unadapted borrowing from German Zeitgeist (literally “spirit of the age”).
